entities.name: Confucius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) was a Chinese philosopher, teacher, and political theorist whose ethical system — built on ren (benevolence), li (ritual propriety), and junzi (the exemplary person) — shaped East Asian civilization for 2,500 years and continues to influence over 1.5 billion people.

Born in the state of Lu during the Spring and Autumn Period, he spent years as a wandering teacher seeking a ruler who would implement his vision of moral governance. His disciples compiled his teachings in the Analerta (Lunyu) — aphorisms on virtue, learning, filial piety, and righteous rule.

Confucius taught that social harmony flows from moral self-cultivation: a sovereign must govern by virtue, not force. He established the 'Five Relationships' (ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger, friend-friend) as society's ethical architecture.

The imperial examination system, based on Confucian texts, governed Chinese bureaucratic selection for over 1,300 years. His thought permeates East Asian cultures, legal traditions, and family structures to this day.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Confucius' teachings shaped East Asian civilization for 2,500 years and continue to influence over 1.5 billion people, with his emphasis on moral governance and social harmony having a profound impact on the development of China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam.
